blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Unit 11 (Trigonometric Functions and their Graphs), arranged by the unit's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each one is solved briefly, step by step.
11.1 Domains and Ranges of Sine and Cosine Functions

blocks.prompt: 1 Define the domain and the range of a function.
blocks.explanation: Domain: the set of all inputs that the function accepts (the values of \(\theta\) for which it has a value). Range: the set of all outputs that the function actually gives. E.g. for \(\sin\theta\): domain \(\mathbb{R}\), range \([-1, 1]\).

book_ref.quote: the set of all inputs that a function accepts

blocks.prompt: 2 Find the domain and range of \(y = \cos x\).
blocks.explanation: For every real \(x\) the terminal side meets the unit circle at exactly one point \(P(x_0, y_0)\), and \(\cos x = x_0\): domain \(\mathbb{R}\). Since \(-1 \le x_0 \le 1\) on the unit circle, range \([-1, 1]\).

book_ref.quote: Thus, the range of sine and cosine functions is

blocks.prompt: 3 Is \(3\sin\theta = 4\) possible for some real \(\theta\)? Give a reason.
blocks.explanation: No. It needs \(\sin\theta = \frac{4}{3} > 1\), but the range of sine is \([-1, 1]\).

book_ref.quote: Use the range to spot impossible equations at once.

blocks.text: 11.1.1 Domains and Ranges of Tangent and Cotangent Functions

blocks.prompt: 4 Find the domain and range of \(\tan\theta\).
blocks.explanation: \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}\) needs \(x \ne 0\), i.e. the terminal side not on the \(Y\)-axis: \(\theta \ne (2n + 1)\frac{\pi}{2}\). Domain \(= \mathbb{R} - \{(2n + 1)\frac{\pi}{2} : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\); range \(= \mathbb{R}\).

book_ref.quote: A fraction has no value when its denominator is

blocks.prompt: 5 Find the domain and range of \(\cot\theta\).
blocks.explanation: \(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y}\) needs \(y \ne 0\), i.e. the terminal side not on the \(X\)-axis: \(\theta \ne n\pi\). Domain \(= \mathbb{R} - \{n\pi : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\); range \(= \mathbb{R}\).

book_ref.quote: For cotangent the denominator is

blocks.prompt: 6 Find all \(\theta\) in \([0, 2\pi]\) where \(\cot\theta\) is undefined and all where \(\tan\theta\) is undefined.
blocks.explanation: \(\cot\theta\) is undefined where \(\sin\theta = 0\): \(\theta = 0, \pi, 2\pi\). \(\tan\theta\) is undefined where \(\cos\theta = 0\): \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}\).

book_ref.quote: Swapping the two lists: tangent fails on the

blocks.text: 11.1.2 Domains and Ranges of Secant Function

blocks.prompt: 7 Find the domain and range of \(y = \sec x\).
blocks.explanation: \(\sec x = \frac{1}{\cos x}\) needs \(\cos x \ne 0\): domain \(\mathbb{R} - \{(2n + 1)\frac{\pi}{2} : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\). For \(0 < \cos x \le 1\), \(\sec x \ge 1\); for \(-1 \le \cos x < 0\), \(\sec x \le -1\): range \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\).

book_ref.quote: So secant and tangent have the same domain.

blocks.prompt: 8 Is \(\sec\theta = \frac{3}{4}\) possible? Give a reason.
blocks.explanation: No. \(\sec\theta = \frac{3}{4}\) would need \(\cos\theta = \frac{4}{3} > 1\), outside the range of cosine; equivalently \(|\sec\theta| \ge 1\) always.

book_ref.quote: Remember the shape of the answer

blocks.text: 11.1.3 Domains and Ranges of Cosecant Function

blocks.prompt: 9 Find the domain and range of \(y = \operatorname{cosec} x\).
blocks.explanation: \(\operatorname{cosec} x = \frac{1}{\sin x}\) needs \(\sin x \ne 0\): domain \(\mathbb{R} - \{n\pi : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\). Since \(0 < |\sin x| \le 1\), \(|\operatorname{cosec} x| \ge 1\): range \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\).

book_ref.quote: so cosecant and cotangent have the same domain

blocks.prompt: 10 Which trigonometric functions have the same domain? Write the three pairs.
blocks.explanation: (1) \(\sin, \cos\): domain \(\mathbb{R}\). (2) \(\tan, \sec\): denominator \(\cos x\), remove \((2n + 1)\frac{\pi}{2}\). (3) \(\cot, \operatorname{cosec}\): denominator \(\sin x\), remove \(n\pi\).

book_ref.quote: The table is easy to remember in three pairs

blocks.prompt: 11 Define an even function and an odd function, with one example of each.
blocks.explanation: \(f\) is even if \(f(-x) = f(x)\) for every \(x\) in its domain (e.g. \(x^{2}\), \(\cos x\)); \(f\) is odd if \(f(-x) = -f(x)\) for every \(x\) in its domain (e.g. \(x^{3}\), \(\sin x\)).

book_ref.quote: A function \(f\) is said to be even if

blocks.prompt: 12 Show that \(\cos\theta\) is an even function and \(\sin\theta\) is an odd function.
blocks.explanation: On the unit circle, the terminal point of \(-\theta\) is the mirror image \((x, -y)\) of \((x, y)\) in the \(x\)-axis. So \(\cos(-\theta) = x = \cos\theta\) (even) and \(\sin(-\theta) = -y = -\sin\theta\) (odd).

book_ref.quote: So one figure proves both results

blocks.prompt: 13 Determine whether \(f(x) = x^{2}\cos x\) is even, odd or neither.
blocks.explanation: \(f(-x) = (-x)^{2}\cos(-x) = x^{2}\cos x = f(x)\). So \(f\) is even.

book_ref.quote: To decide whether a function is even, odd or neither

blocks.prompt: 14 Determine whether \(f(x) = \tan x + x^{3}\) is even, odd or neither.

book_ref.quote: Odd means: changing the sign of the input changes only the sign of the output.

blocks.prompt: 15 Determine whether \(f(x) = 1 + \sin x\) is even, odd or neither.
blocks.explanation: \(f(-x) = 1 - \sin x\). At \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\): \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2\), \(f\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0\), which is neither \(2\) nor \(-2\). So \(f\) is neither even nor odd.

book_ref.quote: Most functions are neither.

blocks.prompt: 16 Show that \(\tan\theta\) is odd and \(\sec\theta\) is even.
blocks.explanation: \(\tan(-\theta) = \dfrac{\sin(-\theta)}{\cos(-\theta)} = \dfrac{-\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = -\tan\theta\) (odd); \(\sec(-\theta) = \dfrac{1}{\cos(-\theta)} = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} = \sec\theta\) (even).

book_ref.quote: The other four functions follow from sine and cosine

blocks.prompt: 17 Define the period of a function. Write the periods of the six trigonometric functions.
blocks.explanation: If \(f(\theta + p) = f(\theta)\) for all \(\theta\) in the domain, the least positive such \(p\) is the period. Periods: \(\sin, \cos, \operatorname{cosec}, \sec\): \(2\pi\); \(\tan, \cot\): \(\pi\).

book_ref.quote: Period of a trigonometric function is the smallest

blocks.prompt: 18 Find the period of \(\cos 6x\).
blocks.explanation: \(\cos(6x + 2\pi) = \cos 6\left(x + \frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \cos 6x\). The value repeats when \(x\) increases by \(\frac{\pi}{3}\): period \(\frac{\pi}{3}\).

book_ref.quote: rewrite the shifted angle

blocks.prompt: 19 Find the period of \(\tan\frac{x}{5}\).
blocks.explanation: \(\tan\left(\frac{x}{5} + \pi\right) = \tan\frac{1}{5}(x + 5\pi) = \tan\frac{x}{5}\): period \(5\pi\).

book_ref.quote: A quick rule that follows from Example 1

blocks.prompt: 20 Find the period of \(4 - 2\sin\frac{\pi x}{3}\).
blocks.explanation: The constant 4 and the factor \(-2\) do not affect the period. \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi x}{3} + 2\pi\right) = \sin\frac{\pi}{3}(x + 6)\): period \(6\).

book_ref.quote: Adding a constant does not change the period.

blocks.prompt: 21 Find the period of \(\cot(4x + 1)\).
blocks.explanation: \(\cot(4x + 1 + \pi) = \cot\left(4\left(x + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) + 1\right) = \cot(4x + 1)\): period \(\frac{\pi}{4}\).

book_ref.quote: runs twice as fast, so the period is halved

blocks.prompt: 22 Show that \(\pi\) is not the period of \(\cos\theta\).
blocks.explanation: \(\cos(\theta + \pi) = -\cos\theta\). For \(\theta = 0\): \(\cos 0 = 1\) but \(\cos\pi = -1\). One counter-example is enough, so \(\pi\) is not the period.

book_ref.quote: One counter-example is enough to reject

blocks.prompt: 25 Find \(\cos 315^{\circ}\) and \(\sin(-150^{\circ})\).

book_ref.quote: The sign follows the quadrant of the angle.

blocks.prompt: 26 Find \(\sec 120^{\circ}\) and \(\operatorname{cosec} 330^{\circ}\).
blocks.explanation: \(\cos 120^{\circ} = -\cos 60^{\circ} = -\frac{1}{2}\), so \(\sec 120^{\circ} = -2\). \(\sin 330^{\circ} = -\sin 30^{\circ} = -\frac{1}{2}\), so \(\operatorname{cosec} 330^{\circ} = -2\).

book_ref.quote: where only sine is positive

blocks.prompt: 27 Write the steps for drawing the graph of a trigonometric function.
blocks.explanation: (i) Make a table of ordered pairs \((x, y)\), \(x\) the angle and \(y\) the value of the function. (ii) Take the angles along the \(X\)-axis. (iii) Take the values along the \(Y\)-axis. (iv) Plot the points. (v) Join them with a smooth curve.

blocks.explanation: Maximum \(1\) at \(x = \frac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi\); minimum \(-1\) at \(x = \frac{3\pi}{2} + 2n\pi\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

blocks.prompt: 29 Where does the graph of \(y = \sin x\) cut the \(x\)-axis in \([-2\pi, 2\pi]\)?

book_ref.quote: exactly where the curve cuts the

blocks.prompt: 30 Why does the graph of \(y = \sin x\) lie between the lines \(y = 1\) and \(y = -1\)?
blocks.explanation: Because \(-1 \le \sin x \le 1\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\): the range of sine is \([-1, 1]\). The curve touches \(y = 1\) at \(\frac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi\) and \(y = -1\) at \(\frac{3\pi}{2} + 2n\pi\).

book_ref.quote: so the graph will be between the horizontal lines

blocks.text: 11.4.3 Graph of y = cos x from - 2pi to 2pi

blocks.prompt: 31 State the maximum and minimum values and the \(x\)-intercepts of \(y = \cos x\).
blocks.explanation: Maximum \(1\) at \(x = n\pi\), \(n\) even; minimum \(-1\) at \(x = n\pi\), \(n\) odd; \(x\)-intercepts at \(x = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

book_ref.quote: Peaks at even multiples of

blocks.prompt: 32 How is the graph of \(y = \cos x\) related to the graph of \(y = \sin x\)?
blocks.explanation: \(\cos x = \sin(x + 90^{\circ})\) (e.g. \(\cos 0^{\circ} = \sin 90^{\circ} = 1\)), so the cosine graph is the sine graph moved \(90^{\circ}\) to the left; same shape, period \(2\pi\), range \([-1, 1]\).

book_ref.quote: so the cosine graph is the sine graph moved

blocks.text: 11.4.4 Graph of y = tan x from -pi to pi

blocks.prompt: 33 Write the asymptotes, the period and the \(x\)-intercepts of \(y = \tan x\) for \(-\pi \le x \le \pi\).
blocks.explanation: Asymptotes \(x = -\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\) (dashed); period \(\pi\); \(x\)-intercepts \(x = -\pi, 0, \pi\).

book_ref.quote: always draw the asymptotes

blocks.prompt: 34 Why is \(\tan 90^{\circ}\) undefined? What happens to \(\tan x\) just left and just right of \(90^{\circ}\)?
blocks.explanation: \(\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\) and \(\cos 90^{\circ} = 0\), so it is undefined. Just left (Quadrant I) \(\tan x \to +\infty\) (\(\tan 89^{\circ} \approx 57.3\)); just right (Quadrant II) \(\tan x \to -\infty\) (\(\tan 91^{\circ} \approx -57.3\)).

book_ref.quote: dividing by a very small number gives a very large answer

blocks.explanation: \(6 + 2\sin x\) runs from \(4\) to \(8\) (positive). Maximum of the reciprocal \(= \frac{1}{4}\), minimum \(= \frac{1}{8}\).

blocks.prompt: 40 A Ferris wheel of radius 15 ft has its lowest point 2 ft above the ground and turns once every 30 seconds. A rider starts at the lowest point. Write a model for the height h(t).
blocks.explanation: \(b = 15\), \(a = 2 + 15 = 17\), \(c = \frac{2\pi}{30} = \frac{\pi}{15}\); start at the bottom: \(h(t) = 17 - 15\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{15}t\right)\). Check: \(h(0) = 2\).

book_ref.quote: the radius gives the amplitude

blocks.prompt: 41 The water level of a river is \(L(t) = 5 + 2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}t\right)\) feet, \(t\) in hours. Find the level at \(t = 2\) and the minimum level.
blocks.explanation: \(L(2) = 5 + 2\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 7\) ft. Minimum \(= 5 - 2 = 3\) ft (when the sine is \(-1\), first at \(t = 6\)).

book_ref.quote: Every problem follows the same plan

blocks.prompt: 42 A quantity varies sinusoidally between a maximum of 20 m and a minimum of 4 m. Find its amplitude and midline.
blocks.explanation: Amplitude \(b = \frac{M - m}{2} = \frac{20 - 4}{2} = 8\) m; midline \(a = \frac{M + m}{2} = \frac{20 + 4}{2} = 12\) m.

book_ref.quote: Model from data: amplitude
